about: Single source of truth for the demo videos: every scene's visual, on-screen action and narration. generate_narration.py turns 'text' into one audio file per scene; build_shot_lists.py turns this file into shot-lists.md. Edit here, then re-run both.

videos.title: The 30-second spiel
videos.notes: Fully animated. No screen recording: the Remotion composition Spiel30 is the whole picture. Drop the five audio clips under it in order.

scenes.text: We're moving our HR data to Databricks. But the rollout only moves tables.

And tables arrive without their meaning. Ask the same table for headcount at the end of Q2, and you get fifty-eight thousand, eight hundred sixty-two. <break time="0.3s" /> Or one hundred seventy-five thousand, five hundred twenty-four. Depending on who writes the query.

scenes.graphic: Spiel30 (part 3: five attritions and a spreadsheet)
scenes.text: Attrition has five versions. And who can see whose salary? That lives in a spreadsheet.
A semantic layer inside of Databricks defines every HR metric, and every access rule, once. So Tableau dashboards, Sequel queries, and AI agents all give the same answer.

scenes.action: None. Hold on the question for two seconds of silence before the end.
scenes.text: The table migration is the foundation. This is the part that delivers trust.

videos.title: The 2-minute proof
videos.notes: Graphics open and close it; the middle is one SQL editor tab. Before recording, open hr_people_analytics/metrics/checks/workforce_checks.sql against the 70,000-person data, with the first two statements changed to show the naive and metric view headcount for 2025-Q2. Run both once so the warehouse is warm, then clear the results.

scenes.text: Our Databricks rollout is moving HR's tables across. What it doesn't move is the definitions. What counts as headcount? What counts as attrition? Who's allowed to see salary? Today, each of those lives in somebody's query, dashboard, or spreadsheet. <break time="0.4s" /> Let's look at an example of what I mean, and how Databricks can solve this, in about a minute. This is Tema, a fictional tech company of about seventy thousand people.

scenes.action: SQL editor, workforce_checks.sql. Put the cursor in the naive query (SUM(headcount) FROM v_headcount_naive, 2025-Q2) and run it. Let the result 175,524 sit on screen.
scenes.text: Here's a query that returns the headcount at the end of the second quarter of twenty twenty-five, straight from the migrated table. <break time="0.3s" /> One hundred seventy-five thousand, five hundred twenty-four. For a company of seventy thousand.

scenes.action: Select (highlight) the SUM(headcount) and GROUP BY in the naive query so the zoom lands on it.
scenes.text: That's what happens when someone adds up April, May, and June. A perfectly reasonable query. The wrong answer. And nothing warns you if this is the query an AI agent writes.

scenes.action: Click into the metric view query (MEASURE(headcount) FROM workforce_metrics, 2025-Q2) and run it. Hover over 58,862.
scenes.text: Same table, same question, through the semantic layer. <break time="0.3s" /> Fifty-eight thousand, eight hundred sixty-two. The rule, headcount is the last month of the period, never a sum, lives in the definition. So nobody can get it wrong. Not in Sequel, not in the dashboard, not in Power BI, and not in Genie.
Has a number like the first one ever reached a leadership deck here?

And headcount is the easy one. Attrition is where it costs money. Once Tema had one definition of attrition, it could finally see that regretted leavers cost about one hundred ninety million dollars a year.

That's the future state. One certified definition per metric, with a named owner. One access rule. And every tool, including AI, reading from it only what the user is allowed to see. The migration is the foundation. This is the part that makes it trustworthy and secure for HR.

videos.title: The 5-minute walk-through
videos.notes: Three proofs, each opened by a SectionCard. Open these tabs first, in this order: (1) workforce_checks.sql as for the 2-minute video; (2) Genie: 'Tema raw (baseline)' and 'HR Tech Analytics Assistant' (the Week 7 'People Analytics Assistant', renamed) in two tabs; (3) governance/02_hrbp_access_activity.sql with step 0 already run so hrbp_a, hrbp_b and manager_m are set; (4) the Workforce Overview dashboard as a fallback. Rebuild the governance model the same day (HRBP scope uses today's date).

scenes.text: We're rolling out Databricks, and Data Engineering is moving our HR tables there. Three things don't move with the tables. What our numbers mean. What AI is allowed to answer. And who's allowed to see sensitive people data. <break time="0.4s" /> Today those live in individual queries, BI tool settings, and spreadsheets. So we manually reconcile numbers before leadership reviews, we're nervous about pointing AI at HR data, and sensitive data access could break at any transfer or reorg. To demonstrate how Databricks can address all of these, the team built a working demo, on a fictional seventy-thousand-person company called Tema. In the next four minutes, you'll learn three ways we're designing Databricks to serve the needs of People Ops.

scenes.graphic: SectionCard 1 before the clip; LowerThird 'Tema is fictional' on the clip
scenes.action: SQL editor, workforce_checks.sql. Run the naive headcount (175,524), pause, then run the metric view headcount (58,862).
scenes.text: First, the numbers don't agree. Here's headcount at the end of the second quarter of twenty twenty-five, from the migrated table. One hundred seventy-five thousand, five hundred twenty-four. <break time="0.3s" /> And here's the same table, same question, through the semantic layer. Fifty-eight thousand, eight hundred sixty-two. Someone, or some AI agent, wrote a valid Sequel query and added up three months. There were neither rules nor context to guide them to the right answer, so they confidently returned the wrong number.

scenes.action: Catalog Explorer: open workspace.tema_hr_semantic, scroll the list of metric views, then open workforce_metrics and show the measures with their comments.
scenes.text: Every metric now has one definition, with an owner. Headcount, hires, leavers, attrition, time to fill, pay, engagement. More than fifteen KPIs across five areas, all in one place.

And because attrition now means precisely one thing, and is defined next to other metrics like time to fill and salary, we can evaluate the cost of regrettable attrition. In our example, Tema lost two thousand, seven hundred eighty-two regretted leavers in the last twelve months. That's about one hundred ninety million dollars a year to replace them, at half a salary each. The AI team alone, which grew about sixfold, accounts for five hundred three of them, at a cost of about sixty-seven million dollars.
If every VP, HRBP, and leader had access to their team's or organization's cost of attrition, what decisions could we make to transform our company?

scenes.action: Genie, two tabs side by side (or record each tab and place them side by side in the editor). Ask both: 'How many people did we have at the end of Q2 2025?' Wait for both answers.
scenes.text: Second, AI gives confident, wrong answers. Here's the same question, asked of Genie on the raw tables, and of our Analytics Assistant on the semantic layer. The raw one adds up the months. The assistant answers fifty-eight thousand, eight hundred sixty-two.

scenes.action: Ask both agents for one named employee's salary (pick the employee in advance). Let the assistant's refusal and its reason stay on screen.
scenes.text: Now ask both for one person's salary. The assistant declines, and says why. The raw one may not.

scenes.graphic: BenchmarkCard (fill in scores in src/data.ts, or skip this graphic)
scenes.text: Same AI, same data. The difference is the definitions and rules underneath. On a twenty-question benchmark, the agent on the semantic layer got far more right than the one on raw tables. AI is only as good as the definitions under it, and the semantic layer is what makes it safe to give HR data to an AI assistant.

scenes.action: 02_hrbp_access_activity.sql: run step 2 (act as hrbp_a), then the 'where can hrbp_a see sensitive data' query by division.
scenes.text: Third, access to sensitive data doesn't follow the org. Here I'm acting as an HR business partner who supports two leaders in different divisions. They see salary and birthdays for everyone in both leaders' whole orgs, and only names and titles for everyone else.

scenes.action: Run step 4 (act as manager_m) and the sample rows query.
scenes.text: Now I'm a people manager. I see my direct reports' birthdays. No salaries.

scenes.action: Run step 6: end one of hrbp_a's assignments, rebuild the scope, rerun the division query. Show the salary counts drop.
scenes.text: And when one of those HR business partner assignments ends, I rebuild, and that access is gone. No tickets. No grant changes.

This dynamic access is just one rule in Unity Catalog. An HR business partner sees sensitive data for the orgs of the leaders they currently support. It's computed from the reporting lines and dated assignments. It handles partners with several leaders, and leaders with several partners. It keeps executives out. And it applies the same way in Sequel, dashboards, BI tools, and Genie. Reorgs fix themselves overnight.

So here's the gap. Today, tables arrive in Databricks, definitions live in people's heads, access lives in a spreadsheet, and AI is off limits or struggles to earn users' trust. <break time="0.4s" /> The future state: every HR number certified once, and the same everywhere. Sensitive data governed by one auditable rule. Definitions changed only by reviewed pull request. And an AI assistant that consistently returns HR data that the business can actually use.
